passage:
Tuesday, late.
Rukmini came home with her maths test today. Seventy-one. Before I could stop myself I said, "Mitra's daughter got ninety-four, you know." Her face shut like a door. She said, "Baba, you always do this," and went to her room without dinner.
I sat with the paper and heard my own father's voice coming out of me. At her age I dropped out of engineering coaching, and some part of me still burns about it. I'm scared she will carry the same regret. That fear is mine, not hers.
The comparison did nothing for her. It only taught her that my warmth depends on a number.
Tomorrow at breakfast I'll tell her I saw her redo the geometry chapter alone on Sunday. That effort was real. I want her to hear that first.
— Anirban

qa.q: What mark did Rukmini get on her maths test?
qa.a: Seventy-one.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling after Rukmini left the table?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid: ashamed that he sounded like his own father, and afraid that Rukmini would carry the same regret he still carries.

qa.q: What does Anirban plan to do differently at breakfast?
qa.a: He plans to praise the real effort he saw, Rukmini redoing the geometry chapter alone, before any talk of marks.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see her Baba's comparison?
qa.a: She likely hears that his love depends on her score, which is why she shut down and skipped dinner instead of trying harder.

grounding: A parent notices that comparing his daughter comes from his own regret and fear, and chooses to praise her effort instead.

Sudha, you asked why I never boast about your marks at family lunches. Let me tell you.
When I was fifteen, my Bua would point at me across the dinner mat and tell her son Manohar, "Look at Chetan, first in class. Why can't you be like him?" Everyone smiled at me. I wanted to sink into my plate. Nobody knew I was failing Hindi and crying over it at night.

Instead I followed him to the terrace and told him about my Hindi marks and my tutor's red ink. He stared, then laughed, and told me about his cricket trials. We stood there until the last rocket went up. Since that night, he has been my closest brother.

Preeti's cheeks went hot. She found Lalit on the back stairs, scrolling nothing on a dead phone.
"She says that every time," Lalit said flatly. "Enjoy it."

Lalit looked up. "You? Seriously?"
"Seriously. And I can't dance. You saw."
He snorted. The generator finally caught, and yellow light spilled over them.
"Don't tell Mausi," Preeti said.

The bus had been stuck in the flooded underpass for forty minutes, and the board exam form was due at the school office before five. Afreen stared at the rain.
"Your Ammi called my Ammi again," Madhuri said carefully. "About Sameera's ranks."
Afreen shrugged. "Let her. I don't care anymore." She hadn't opened her chemistry book in two weeks. Every time Ammi mentioned Sameera, Afreen simply switched off, like a fan.
Madhuri waited. "Don't care, or don't want to feel it?"
Afreen opened her mouth to snap back, then didn't. Her throat was tight. "It still hurts," she said at last, very quietly. "I just stopped showing it. And stopped studying."
The bus lurched forward. Afreen checked the time: they would make it, barely.
"Tonight," she said, "I'm going to tell Ammi what the Sameera talk does to me. Just once, properly."

Papa took the last of his books to the new flat today. The shelf in the hall looks like a mouth with missing teeth. I kept thinking of Sunday mornings when the three of us made dosas and fought over the crispy ones. That family is gone, and I didn't get a vote.

Jomon, sit. You slammed the door on your father this morning, and I know that feeling well.
When I was sixteen, my parents separated. I decided it was all my father's fault. He had been the one who shouted, so to me he was the villain. On his visits I went up to the terrace and stayed there until his scooter left. For a whole year I would not sit in one room with him.
Then my Chithi, my mother's younger sister, found me up there one evening. She asked, "Rashmi, are you angry, or are you sad?" I started to say angry, and burst into tears instead.
Later I learned there were things neither of them had told me, on both sides. I still don't know the whole story, and that's fine. What I know is this: I nearly lost a father over a story I had half-written myself.

The bus strike meant there was only one way to reach cousin Tanu's engagement in Nagpur: three hours in Papa's small car. Madhuri took the back seat, as far from him as possible, earphones in and music off.
Since he moved out, she had refused every dinner with him. He broke our home, she kept telling herself.

Papa's hands tightened on the wheel. He looked old, Madhuri thought suddenly, and tired, not like a villain.
She took out one earphone. The anger felt thinner than it had at home, and underneath it was something heavier, a sadness she hadn't let herself feel.
"I'm not ready to talk about it," she said. "But I'll come for dinner on Sunday." Papa nodded without turning around.

Every morning that week, Leila made her bed before her alarm went off. She ironed her school shirt, finished her homework on the tram, and brought home a spelling test with full marks, which she left carefully on the kitchen table in their Lyon apartment.
Her father, Marek, noticed. On Thursday he found her scrubbing the bathroom sink at ten at night.
"Leila. What's going on?"
She kept scrubbing. "If I don't argue, and my grades are good, maybe Maman will come back."
Marek sat on the edge of the bath. The next evening Maman came over, and the three of them sat at the kitchen table.
"We are separating because of us," Maman said slowly. "Not because of your grades, not because of any fight you had with anyone. Nothing you did."
"Nothing," Marek repeated. "You can stop being perfect. We both love you exactly the same."
Leila put her head down on the table and finally cried.

qa.a: On the kitchen table in their Lyon apartment.

qa.q: Why was Leila scrubbing the sink so late at night?

Coach's note, under-18 hockey, 14 March
Parul arrived early today and stayed after practice to help the juniors, as she has most weeks this term. Last autumn she missed games and snapped at teammates when her parents were separating. Her younger brother Tejas, who plays in the under-12 squad, told me then that home was "very loud."
Today, while we packed cones, she told me plainly that her parents are happier living apart. She is at her father's place on Saturdays and her mother's the rest of the week, and she arranges her match schedule around both. She said she tells them honestly when a weekend feels hard.
I asked whether she still feels sad. She paused, then said, "Sometimes, yes. I let it be sad now." That sounded honest, not forced.
Next step: I'll keep up our Friday check-ins and let the school counsellor know she's doing well.

passage:
So you asked how I got through Class 12. Honestly? Barely. I'm Hemant, by the way, for anyone just tuning in.
When my parents split, Papa got custody for the school year. He was in his own fog. He forgot parent-teacher day. He forgot I'd told him my board dates. Once I came home from a chemistry paper and there was nothing to eat, not even bread.
For a while I thought, maybe I'm just not worth remembering. That was the worst part.
Then one night I wrote my exam dates on a big sheet and taped it to the fridge. I told him, "Papa, I need you to see this every day." He looked at it for a long time and said, "I've been failing you, son, haven't I."
And I started going to my Dadi's flat, two streets away, for dinner. She'd ask about every paper.
That's how. One sheet on the fridge, and one grandmother.

qa.q: Where did Hemant tape the exam dates?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Papa kept forgetting things?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and unimportant, even wondering whether he was worth remembering at all.

qa.q: What helped Hemant most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Papa clearly with the sheet on the fridge, and leaning on Dadi for dinners and interest in his papers, gave him both attention and care.

qa.q: How does Papa seem to feel when he sees the sheet on the fridge?
qa.a: He seems shaken and regretful, realising for the first time how much he has neglected his son during his own pain.

grounding: A teen whose father forgot his meals and exams during the divorce asks clearly for what he needs and leans on his grandmother.
